![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/02bec11dec3fc03b97b918c392969b246e6b2751d78c0b32b796bdeb4e6eaaca.png)

The graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)$, the derivative of a continuous function $y=f(x)$, is given above. Which of the following could be the graph of $y=f(x)?$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that critical points of $y=f(x)$ occur when ${f}^{′}(x)=0$ or ${f}^{′}(x)$ does not exist. In our case, there is one critical point:  

$\,$ $x=-1$  

Also, we have the following: 

- If ${f}^{′}(x)>0$ then $f(x)$ is increasing.

- If ${f}^{′}(x)<0$ then $f(x)$ is decreasing.

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below.

| $x$ | $(-\infty ,-1)$ | $-1$ | $(-1,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${f}^{′}$ | $-$ | $0$ | $+$ |
| $f$ | $↘$ | $\text{min}$ | $↗$ |

Let's now sketch the graph of $y=f(x):$

- First, we draw the critical points. Consider the vertical line $x=-1$ and choose an arbitrary point on it.

$\,$ So, we draw it as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/9062dcd04f6ca0dcb21453596ebd007ccf91a33f5092a601d24e401e888a20f1.png)

- Next, we consider the behavior of $y=f(x)$ in the neighborhood of the critical points:

- Since $f(x)$ is decreasing $↘$ on $(-\infty ,-1)$ and increasing $↗$ on $(-1,\infty )$, the graph of $f(x)$ goes up to the left and to the right of $x=-1.$

- Moreover, since ${f}^{′}(x)$ is increasing to the left of $x=2$ and to the right of $x=2$, although with different slopes, we must have ${f}^{″}(x)>0.$ So, the curve $y=f(x)$ is concave up on $(-\infty ,2)$  and on $(2,\infty ).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/fbd0da8fbd98e0b83cd1efb82d5e1f1aca1bf40108e11c6a401da46e514a133a.png)

- Finally, since we are told that our graph must be continuous, by connecting and extending the existing parts with a smooth curve, we obtain a possible graph of $y=f(x):$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/95cc3ce5bab09a3e3ea32571e2156d13605b85bf8f026c7c35b5dd51d045c7fd.png)

**Note:** The graph we obtained is not the only possible one. Any similar graph that's shifted vertically up or down could also be considered a possible $y=f(x).$
